INFORMATION
#32777588                                                                         2005
SKPC 71

IN THE PROVINCIAL COURT
FOR SASKATCHEWAN

SASKATOON, SASKATCHEWAN

BETWEEN:

HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN

- and -

LEON EPP

D. Black                                                                                               For
the Crown

W. Towstego                                                                                       For
the Defendant

Notice:
Pursuant to
s.486(3)
of the
Criminal Code
the Court ordered a ban on
publication or broadcast of the identity of the complainant or any information
that could disclose the identity of the complainant in these proceedings.

August 22, 2005

S. P. Whelan, PCJ

Reasons

Introduction and Issues

[
1
]        Mr. Epp was
found guilty after a trial of one count of sexual assault contrary to section
271 of the Code.  I suspended the passing of sentence and placed him on
probation for 1 year. The conditions included: an approved residence, no
contact with the complainant, addictions assessment, education, counselling, or
treatment as recommended, and personal counselling and/or sex offender
programming. The Crown made application pursuant to
s. 490.012(1)
of the

Criminal Code
for an order requiring him to comply with the provisions of the
Sex Offender Information Registration Act (SOIRA). The defence raised two
issues:

i)          Does an order pursuant to s. 490.012(1) of the Code have
retrospective application where the offence was committed prior to the Act
taking effect and the offender has yet to be sentenced?

ii)         Should the court grant the offender’s application and decline
to order registration having regard to the test found in s. 490.012(4) of the
Code?

I declined the Crown’s
application and undertook to provide my written reasons at a later date.
Reasons are required pursuant to s. 490.012(5) of the Code.  I found it
unnecessary to address the first issue in light of my decision to grant the
offender’s application on the merits.

Background Circumstances

[
2
]        These are the
facts as I found them on the trial matter:

The complainant and the
accused had been neighbours for 3 or 4 months. She helped him collect bottles
and on two of these occasions he helped her learn to drive. She was 15 years of
age at the time and he is now 54 years old.

Earlier that evening he drove
her out of the city to visit one of her friends and she had helped him search
for bottles in several locations. Around 11 p.m. he asked her to go for a
drive. He drove into a field and offered her a drink of whiskey. They sat and
talked for a while. She felt he became “kind of drunk” and observed that he was
slurring his words.  She had one drink of alcohol. He repeatedly asked her to
remove her bra and she repeatedly declined. He asked her to lean forward and
she asked why and he said just do it. When she did, he reached his hand under
the back of her shirt and undid her bra.

Her reaction was immediate.
She did up her bra and demanded to be taken home. He declined and told her to
stay calm. She moved to the driver’s seat of the vehicle and drove from the
field onto a road and down to the highway. He reached over, turned the car off,
and threw the keys out the window. She got out of the car and began walking. He
found the keys and followed her in the vehicle and repeatedly told her to get
in. At one point he grabbed her pants and tried to pull her into the car. He
then offered that he wouldn’t touch or talk to her and would drive her home if
she would just get into the vehicle. She was concerned about being out on the
highway late at night and having to walk into the city so she got into the back
seat and he drove her home.

Once home she phoned the
police and made a complaint. She was aware that he had a hearing problem.

[
3
]        For the purpose
of sentence, I find that there was no evidence that Mr. Epp’s persistence
following the sexual assault, was with a view to continuing the sexual assault.
Once he convinced the complainant that he intended her no further harm, she consented
to his driving her home.

[
4
]        The
pre-sentence report provided pertinent background information. Mr. Epp was an
“RH” baby and was born with disabilities. He grew up on the family farm in a
protected environment but at age 16 was sent to live in Saskatoon where he
attended the Crippled Children’s Council. There is some suggestion in the
report that he may be somewhat mentally challenged. He married in 1974 and
divorced in 1978. He is the father of two children from that marriage but has
little contact with the one surviving offspring. He has lived in a common law
relationship since 1980. His partner, who was described as being financially
and socially dependent upon Mr. Epp, remains supportive and he has supportive
friends.

[
5
]        Mr. Epp has
many health-related issues. He is very hard of hearing and it is deteriorating.
He has not adapted to hearing aids. He lipreads.  He is without teeth. He is
awaiting surgery for a cataract. He was involved in a car accident recently and
incurred a wound to his head requiring 136 stitches. He has suffered nerve
damage to his face. He believes that a hip might have to be replaced. He can
appear awkward in his walk as he has a problem with his limbs.

[
6
]        He has two
prior convictions for drinking and driving in 1980 and 1991. He told the
probation officer that he quit drinking after the first conviction and didn’t
drink again except on the occasion of the second driving offence and the
current offence. He has promised not to drink anymore. According to his partner
he drank only a few times over the years. She reported that alcoholism runs in
the family and that Leon “shouldn’t drink”.

[
7
]        Mr. Epp has a
grade 9 education. He reports being able to read and write quite well. He likes
woodworking and makes small items which he sells to augment his income. He
completed a job training program about a year ago and has worked briefly as a
security guard. He supplements his income by picking bottles and has made up to
$600.00 per month in this fashion. He and his partner have been cut off social
assistance as he received a small inheritance and he fears doing without
assistance as most of the inheritance has been spent.

[
8
]        He reported to
the probation officer that he hadn’t drank that much alcohol on the occasion of
this offence and that he knew what he was doing. He acknowledged having had
many sexual thoughts about the complainant prior to the offence. He has made
many excuses for the offence including that he believed he had consent. However
the probation officer offered that his approach may be attributed to a poor
choice of words and his “way of thinking sexually”, given his limited life
experiences.

[
9
]        The probation
officer conducted three risk assessments. While I have expressed concerns in
the past regarding the use of risk assessments in pre-sentence reports
concerning adults, (
see
R. v. Hildebrandt
2005 SKPC 35
) I refer to these
assessments because they are in keeping with my view that the risk to re-offend
sexually is low. Using the ORAMS risk assessment he was found to be a “medium
risk to re-offend” generally. The tool used was said to be of little assistance
as it is “generally recognized in the research that measures used to predict
general recidivism are not very effective in predicting sexual recidivism”. The
Static-99 was employed to predict sexual recidivism. He was found to be a low
risk to re-offend sexually and in fact scored “1” on the test (between the 1
st

and 23
rd
percentile). The author also administered the Stable 2000
Risk Assessment, stating that the purpose of the assessment is “to be attentive
to rationalizations, justifications, attitudes and beliefs which impact on the
current offence and those that must be addressed in treatment in order to
facilitate change”.

[
10
]      With respect to
the issue of “sexual self regulation”, the author stated: “While Leon is 55 and
D. was 15, there does not appear to be an overt repetitive interest in young
girls to warrant having Leon evaluated as having a deviant sexual interest.
Although he has engaged in sexually deviant behaviour, he prefers sexual
activity with consenting adults.”

[
11
]      With respect to
“attitudes tolerant of sexual assault” the author stated: “This is an area that
Leon needs to spend some time examining and learning new information. . .His
attitudes and beliefs about women, what they wear, how they behave, influence
the decisions he makes based on what he knows of women, men and relationships,
and come from questionable and totally wrong information.”

[
12
]      The probation
officer proposed some introductory information sessions on alcohol abuse and
sexual offender programming. The officer also proposed a curfew which I did not
impose. He had been subject to a curfew from September 2003 until February
2005. Further as he was not viewed as a predator, it was not necessary to
monitor his movement in the community.

[
13
]      A victim impact
statement was made available to the court. The complainant acknowledged that
others may think that the offence was minor but expressed that it caused her to
think about what could have happened. It has affected her feelings about
herself and her willingness to trust others. She experienced depression. It
affected her relationships and her school and work.

Reasoning

[
14
]      I have referred
to the following cases in my reasons:

R. v. Casaway
[2005] N.W.T. No. 30
(NWTSC),

R. v. Clarke
[2005] N.S.J. No. 206
(N.S.S.C.)

R. v. Have
[2005] O.J. No. 388
,
2005
ONCJ 27

R. v. Dyck
(2004),
2004 ONCJ 103 (CanLII)
,
187 C.C.C. (3d) 73
(Ont. C.J.)

R. v. Jordan
2002 NSCA 11 (CanLII)
,
[2002] N.S.J. No. 20
(N.S.C.A.)

R.E.M.

2005 BCSC 698 (CanLII)
,
[2005] B.C.J. No. 1191
(B.C.S.C.)

R. v. B.(S.A.)
(2003),
231 D.L.R. (4th)
602
,
2003 SCC 60

Baron v. Canada
(1993),
1993 CanLII 154 (SCC)
,
78 C.C.C. (3d) 510
(S.C.C.)

R. v. Rouschop
[2005] O.J. No. 1336 (Ont
Court of Justice)

R. v. Worm
2005 ABPC 92 (CanLII)
,
[2005] A.J. No. 434
(Provincial Court)

R. v. Woodburn
[2005] O.J. No. 391
,
2005
ONCJ 30

R. v. Jepson
[2004] O.J. No. 5521

(Ontario Superior Court of Justice)

The Appendix to this
decision provides excerpts of the
Criminal Code
and the Sex Offender
Information Registration Act.

Should the Court grant the
offender’s application and decline to order registration having regard to the
test found in s. 490.012(4)?

[
15
]      A sexual assault
committed contrary to s. 271 of the Code is a designated offence within the
definition provided in paragraph a) of s. 490.011(1). Section  s. 490.012(5)
directs that I provide written reasons.

[
16
]      In
R. v.
Casaway, supra,
Schuler J.  reviewed the intent of the registry, the
guiding principles, the type of information to be collected, the restrictions
on access, use and disclosure of the information in the registry, and
protection of the privacy of the registrant. The court provided a helpful
summary of the legislation and remarked upon the nature of the onus on the
applicant.

“¶ 6      As far as being identified as a
sex offender to the community, it is clear that is not the purpose of the Act.
The purpose is set out in s. 2(1): to help police services investigate crimes
of a sexual nature by requiring the registration of certain information
relating to sex offenders. The Act recognizes a number of principles in s.
2(2), among them that

(c) the privacy interests of sex offenders
and the public interest in their rehabilitation and reintegration into the
community as law‑abiding citizens require that

(i) the information be collected only to
enable police services to investigate crimes that there are reasonable grounds
to suspect are of a sexual nature, and

(ii)  access to the
information, and use and disclosure of it, be restricted.

¶ 7      The information to be collected
under the Act relates to addresses of home and work, telephone numbers, height,
weight and physical distinguishing marks. Record is also kept of the sexual
offence or offences for which the registration order was made, the age and
gender of the victim or victims of each offence and the sex offender's
relationship to each victim.

¶ 8      There is no provision in the Act
for the publication of information collected to the community at large. There
are a number of provisions in the Act aimed at keeping the registration and
information confidential and restricting the use of same. For example, when a
copy of the s. 490.012 order is sent to the police service whose member charged
the sex offender with the offence that gave rise to the order, under s. 8(1)(b)
of the Act, the person who registers information for the police service shall
ensure that registration is done in a manner and in circumstances that ensure
its confidentiality. When a sex offender reports to a registration centre and
information is collected from him, the person who collects the information must
ensure that the sex offender's privacy is respected in a manner that is
reasonable in the circumstances and that the information is provided and
collected in a manner and in circumstances that ensure its confidentiality: s.
9. A person who registers the information collected is also required under s.
10 of the Act to ensure that registration of the information is done in a
manner and in circumstances that ensure its confidentiality.

¶ 9      Section 16 of the Act provides
that only certain persons may consult information collected under the Act;
these are mainly persons who would work in the collection, registration and
maintenance of the information and police officers investigating sexual
offences. There is some authority given to the Commissioner of the Royal
Canadian Mounted Police to authorize access to the information for research or
statistical purposes under certain conditions.

¶ 10      There are also restrictions put
on disclosure and use of information collected. Any contravention of the
sections of the Act that provide for who may consult the information and by
whom and for what purposes it may be disclosed or used is a summary conviction
offence for which the person convicted is liable to a fine of not more than
$10,000.00 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than six months, or to
both: s. 17(2).

¶ 11      I am satisfied on reviewing the
Act that it does not have as a purpose the dissemination of information to the
community at large and that its provisions indicate an intention to keep
information collected confidential and for use only by those with a legitimate
reason in keeping with the purposes of investigation of crime and protection of
society.

¶ 12      Under s. 490.012 (4) of the

Criminal Code
, the onus is on Mr. Casaway to satisfy me that if the order is
made, the impact on his privacy would be grossly disproportionate to the public
interest in society's protection by effective investigation of sexual crimes by
means of the Act. While registration will certainly have some impact on his
privacy, I have to balance that against the purpose of the legislation and its
confidentiality requirements. I also take into account that Mr. Casaway has now
been convicted of sexual assault twice. The standard of "grossly
disproportionate" is very high, more than just disproportionate. I find
that Mr. Casaway has not met the onus.

¶ 13      Mr. Casaway also has the onus of
satisfying me that the order sought would have a grossly disproportionate
impact on his liberty.”

[
17
]      In
R. v.
Clarke, supra,
detailed facts surrounding the offence are not available.
The charges were sexual interference contrary to s.151 and sexual touching
contrary to s.152. He was sentenced to 6 months incarceration followed by one year
of probation on each count, concurrent to each other, but consecutive to the
sentence he was then serving on an unrelated offence. Gruchy J. reviewed other
reported decisions in which orders had been granted and concluded that the case
fell at the low end of the continuum of sexual offences, however the order
requiring registration was granted. The court conducted a rather helpful
discussion having regard to the effect of the reporting requirements upon the
offender, beginning at paragraph 9:

“¶ 9      In his submissions defence
counsel states, correctly in my view, that registration will have certain far‑reaching
effects upon the offender. It will require annual reporting and more frequently
after his release whenever he moves, if he should go to the United States or
upon any change of his employment. At the time of reporting he may be
questioned about his job, with whom he is living, about the offence, all of
which will be a considerable intrusion to his liberty and privacy.

. . .

¶ 18      I have considered the reporting
requirements of the Act and I conclude that while they are not onerous the
requirement is for a very long period of time ‑ in this case 20 years
from the date of the Order. That is certainly a factor which bears heavily on
my consideration. Justice Duncan said
in
R. v. Have
,
2005 ONCJ 27 (CanLII)
,
[2005] O.J. No.
388
:

... Subjecting the individual to an
obligation for ten years (in this case twenty years) enforceable by prosecution
and imprisonment is, in itself, a significant infringement on liberty. The subject
is required to provide information that he otherwise could keep private and to
which the state would have no right of access. I agree with

Hearn J.

. . .

¶ 20      Justice Duncan expressed a
concern of mine in the following when considering the phrase "grossly
disproportionate"

Grossly disproportionate:

Having assessed the impact of the proposed
Order on the offender and the public interest to be served by registration, I
must consider whether the former is grossly disproportionate to the latter. On
the face of it, this test appears almost impossible for a defendant to meet.
However in my view, this section must be given an interpretation that results
in some meaningful leeway for a defendant to demonstrate that he should not be
included.

...

Providing a hearing and an opportunity to
present one's case is meaningless if the exception is so narrow that the making
of the Order is, for all practical purposes, mandatory. Any right of appeal is
similarly meaningless. Beyond those concerns, even from a public interest point
of view it is desirable that the registry not be so inclusive as to include so
many low risk or no risk offenders as to dilute the resources and attention of
the police from those that pose a genuine risk.

¶ 21      The phrase "grossly
disproportionate" as noted by Justice Duncan was considered by our Court
of Appeal in relation to the D.N.A. databank legislation
in
R. v. Jordan
,

(2002)
2002 NSCA 11 (CanLII)
,
1 C.R. (6th) 141
, when Cromwell, J.A. said:

In what circumstances would the impact of
the order on the offender's privacy and security of the person be grossly
disproportionate to the public interest in the protection of society and the
proper administration of justice to be achieved through the early detection,
arrest and conviction of offenders? In my view, this will be so if two factors
are present. The first involves a comparison of the balance struck by
Parliament in the legislation for the majority of cases on the one hand and the
particular circumstances of the case before the Court on the other. If the
circumstances of the particular offender or of the offence or of the risk of
breach of privacy or security of the person vary markedly from the sort of
cases which Parliament may be presumed to have had in mind in devising the
legislative scheme, the impact of the order may be found to be grossly
disproportionate ...”

[
18
]
In
R. v.
Have
, supra,
after pleading guilty to possession of child pornography, the
offender was again found in possession of child pornography. The material had
been in his possession at the time of his first arrest but was not known to the
police. Beginning at paragraph 12 Duncan J. discussed the impact of
registration upon the offender generally and on the individual before the
court:

“Impact on the defendant:

¶ 12      In my opinion, the impact of an
Order on any offender, including the defendant, is substantial. Subjecting the
individual to an obligation for ten years enforceable by prosecution and
imprisonment is, in itself, a significant infringement on liberty. The subject is
required to provide information that he otherwise could keep private and to
which the state would have no right of access.
I agree with Hearn J. in
Dyck

that there is substantial stigma attaching to an individual who is subject to
registration, even if only in his mind. It may undermine treatment,
rehabilitation and re‑integration into the community. Finally, I would
add that there may be a fine line between the legitimate police
"tracking" of offenders and the harassing of them. There is no
control against harassment except the judgment and restraint of the local
police force.

¶ 13      These features of the impact of
an Order are common to all offenders. The defendant is subject to some
additional impact in that on the making of an Order, he is labeled a "sex
offender," a somewhat inaccurate and more stigmatic label than his crime
might otherwise be thought to carry. Moreover, he is put into the same basket
and subjected to the same restraints and obligations as those who have
committed much more serious crimes.”

The court denied the
Crown’s application, stating that while the offence was a designated offence it
was the only offence that did not necessarily involve an act of a sexual nature
against a direct victim and as such was not an offence of a sexual nature
within the meaning of the Sex Offender Information Registration Act
.
The
offender was found to be a low risk to re-offend and the impact of registration
was found to be substantial and in this case grossly disproportionate.  In
reaching its decision, the court drew upon the jurisprudence with respect to
the similarly worded provision for an exception to the otherwise mandatory DNA
order pursuant to s.487.051(2),
discussed in
R. v. Jordan
, supra.

[
19
]
The case of

R.E.M.

supra,
involved three historical charges of sexual assault
and indecent assault in relation to a step daughter, spanning a period of 7
years when the victim was between the ages of 9 and 16. The offender received a
total of 18 months incarceration. Romilly, J. declined to order the offender to
register, having determined that the public interest in such an order was to
further public safety, prevent crimes of a predatory sexual nature and to aid
in investigation. It was determined that there was minimal public interest
given that the offences occurred 28 years earlier, and he had not offended
before or since. Having reviewed section 490.012(4), the court expressed the
issues in this way:

“¶ 63      It seems clear that in embarking
on an analysis under s. 490.012(4) the courts must deal with three issues,
namely the impact on the defendant, the public interest served by registration,
and finally whether the impact is grossly disproportionate to the public
interest.”

[
20
]      Romilly, J.
considered the impact of registration upon the privacy and security of the
offender, referring first to
R. v. Have
, supra,
and then, at paragraph
65, to a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada with respect to a DNA order
in

R. v. B. (S.A.)
, supra:

“¶ 65      This viewpoint must be
contrasted however with the statement of
the Supreme Court of Canada in the
case of
R. v. B.(S.A.)

(2003),
231 D.L.R. (4th) 602
,
2003 SCC 60
, where it was
held in relation to an order for DNA that privacy concerns have less of an
impact on convicted criminals as they have a reduced expectation of privacy.
This concept was explained by Rosenberg J.A. in a passage of R. v. Hendry,
supra that was subsequently adopted in British Columbia
in the cases of R. v.
Ku
(2002),
2002 BCCA 559 (CanLII)
,
169 C.C.C. (3d) 535 (B.C.C.A.)
and R. v. S.A.M.,
[2003] B.C.J. No.
2451
,
2003 BCCA 561
. Rosenberg J. held in relation to DNA orders at para. 18:

The legislation offers significant
protections against misuse of the DNA profile information, thus minimizing an
improper intrusion into the offender's privacy. Having been convicted of a
designated offence, the offender already has a reduced expectation of privacy.
In the ordinary case of an adult offender the procedures for taking the sample
have no, or at worst, a minimal impact on the security of the person. Thus, in
the case of an ordinary adult offender there are important state interests
served by the DNA data bank and few reasons based on privacy and security of
the person for refusing to make the order.”’

[
21
]      Beginning at
paragraph 66
in
R. v. R.E.M.
,
the court considered the public interest
which is intended to be served by the
Sex Offender Information Registration
Act
and turned to paragraph 15 of
R. v. Have
, supra,
and the
discussion about the purpose of the Act:

“¶ 67
The case of
Have
, supra also
addresses the above purpose and goes on to hold at para. 15:

The purpose and value of the legislation is
not limited to that statement but rather includes other purposes that are
served by the scheme created by the Act. (
see
R. v. Jordan
infra at para.
34
).
Those purposes are essentially the same as those served by Christopher's Law,
so I think it is fair to borrow from the evidence heard
in the
Dyck
case,
paragraphs
27‑29
. There is an aspect of crime prevention in that
registration in itself is thought to act as a deterrent to potential offenders.
But the main purpose of registration is to further public safety by permitting
police to keep track of sex offenders living or working in the local community.
This information may be useful in the investigation of future sex related
crimes by identifying individuals who, by reason of past convictions, may be
considered suspect  in such crimes. The model is the predatory stranger
offender who "hunts" from areas close to his home or work.
Registration is particularly valuable to enable quick response in cases of
child abduction by a stranger, where time is of the essence to prevent murder.”

[
22
]      Romilly J.
addressed the third issue; whether the impact of registration would be grossly
disproportionate to the public interest served by the registry. He looked at
the approach taken in the judgment of Cromwell J.A.
in
R. v. Jordan
, supra
,
which was concerned with the DNA legislation. Justice Cromwell in turn adopted
the approach taken by
the Supreme Court of Canada in
Baron v. Canada
, supra
,
which was also concerned with the impact of ordering that a DNA sample be
taken. Cromwell J.A. stated:

“¶ 61      Sopinka, J.
in
Baron
[See Note
42 below] identified three factors relevant to the balancing of the
individual's right to be free from state intrusion and the societal interest in
law enforcement.  They were, broadly stated, the nature of the offence, the
nature of the intrusion and the circumstances of the individual who will be the
subject of the intrusion.  These provide a useful starting point for
consideration of whether, in a particular case, the impact of the taking of DNA
samples on the offender's privacy and security of the person will be grossly
disproportionate to the state's law enforcement objectives.  These factors, of
course, cannot be considered in isolation from each other; it is the overall
balance that is critical.”

[
23
]      In the context
of ordering DNA samples, Cromwell J.A. discussed factors that should be
considered when embarking on an analysis of whether an order would be grossly
disproportionate, including: the criminal record of the person, the nature of
the offence, the circumstances surrounding its commission, and evidence as to
the potential impact of an order on the person's privacy and security of the
person.
See
R. v. Jordan
, supra
, beginning at paragraph 63.

[
24
]      Before leaving
R.
v. Jordan

and the approach
taken with respect to the DNA legislation, it is
worthwhile to consider further Justice Cromwell’s discussion of the purpose of
the DNA legislation and the significance of a criminal record and the risk to
re-offend, beginning at paragraph 64. Justice Cromwell points out that the
identification of offenders is not the only purpose of the legislation, hence
an offender who is unlikely to re-offend does not necessarily fall outside the
intended purpose of the provisions. One of the purposes is to eliminate
innocent persons. Secondly he points out that it is implicit in the legislative
scheme that individualized grounds to believe that the person will re-offend
are not required and therefore not part of the balance that Parliament sought
to strike. When one considers the intent of the SOIRA, it would seem that the
purpose of the legislation is very much tied to the identification of
offenders. This is seen as a means of assisting in the investigation of
offences of a sexual nature. It is implicit in the SOIRA, I believe, that the
identification assists in the investigation of offences where an individual has
offended previously, has been identified and offends again. Information about
offenders, generally, is perhaps of assistance in eliminating innocent persons,
however the major purpose in collecting this information is to assist in
identifying the perpetrator
of a subsequent offence.

[
25
]      Having regard to
this application pursuant to s.490.12(4) of the Code, I must be satisfied that
registration under the
Sex Offender Information Registration Act
would
have an impact on the offender, including his privacy or liberty, which would
be grossly disproportionate to the public interest in protecting society
through effective investigation of sexual offences, as may be achieved by such
registration.

[
26
]      I plan to
consider this question in much the same manner as Romilly J. did
in
R. v.
R.E.M.
, supra
, beginning with 3 questions:

a) What is the
impact on the individual offender,

b) What is the
public interest served by registration, and

c) Is the impact upon the defendant grossly disproportionate to the
public interest having regard to:

i)  the nature
of the offence,

ii) the nature
of the intrusion, and

iii) the
circumstances of the individual offender.

[
27
]      As
stated in
R.
v. Jordan
, supra
by Cromwell J.A. the answer to the 3
rd
question
involves a consideration of the balance intended by the legislation and a
comparison of the majority of cases on the one hand and the particular
circumstances of the case before the court on the other. If the circumstances
of this case vary markedly from the cases Parliament may be presumed to have

b) What is the public
interest served by registration?

[

considered in

R.E.M.

“¶ 15      The legislation's purpose is to
assist police investigation of sexual crimes, to collect and maintain current
accurate information all the while respecting the privacy interests of sex

basis. In contrast to similar legislation in the United States, the information
is not publicly disseminated (See Alaska Sex Offender Registration Act, for

[
38

[

pertaining to sex offenders. Section 2(2) provides that the Act is to be

- effective investigation, requires rapid access to certain information
about sex offenders,

-  collection and
registration of information must be current and reliable, and

-

- information be

, and

- access to,

[

in

, supra

registration itself would act as a deterrent to potential offenders. He stated
that the assumption underlying the scheme is that a person who has committed
this type of offence in the past may have a propensity to commit a similar
offence in the future:

“The public interest to be served by
registration:

¶ 14      The stated purpose of the
registry can be found in the statement of purpose in section 2 of the SOIR Act:

2(1) The purpose of this Act is to help
police services investigate crimes of a sexual nature by requiring the
registration of certain information relating to sex offenders.

¶ 15      The purpose and value of the
legislation is not limited to that statement but rather includes other purposes
that are served by the scheme created by the Act. (
see
R. v. Jordan
infra at
para.
34
). Those purposes are essentially the same as those served by
Christopher's Law, so I think it is fair to borrow from the evidence heard
in
the
Dyck

27‑29
. There is an aspect of crime prevention
in that registration in itself is thought to act as a deterrent to potential
offenders. But the main purpose of registration is to further public safety by
permitting police to keep track of sex offenders living or working in the local
community. This information may be useful in the investigation of future sex
related crimes by identifying individuals who, by reason of past convictions,
may be considered suspect in such crimes. The model is the predatory stranger
offender who "hunts" from areas close to his home or work.
Registration is particularly valuable to enable quick response in cases of
child abduction by a stranger, where time is of the essence to prevent murder.

¶ 16      In summary, the assumption
underlying the scheme is that a person who has committed this type of offence
in the past may have a propensity to commit a similar offence in the future.
Registration of such persons is valuable in cases of offences committed locally
by strangers to the victim. The value of a registry to investigation of other
types of sex related offences is less apparent.”

[
41
]      The information
requirements of the Act are aimed at effectively identifying the sex offender,
recording the nature of the offences committed, and tracking his/her current
whereabouts. I agree with Justice Duncan that as well as serving the purpose of

those who would offend, particularly those who are registered under the Act.
Having considered the discussion of the impact of the legislation from the

Have
and Clarke,
decisions

[

successful investigation of crimes of a sexual nature. There is the additional,
albeit somewhat lesser, interest in protection through deterrence. The question
remains whether, having regard to this analysis, the public has an interest in
this offender being required to register.

i)  the nature of the
offence

[
57
]      The Crown
proceeded summarily. The facts of the offence, referred to above at paragraphs

between the offender, age 54, and the victim, age 15, there was nothing about

reported to the probation officer that he had been having sexual thoughts about

ii) the nature of the
intrusion

[
58
]      I am mindful of
R.
v. B. (S.A.)
, infra
, concerning the DNA legislation, in which the Supreme
Court of Canada remarked on the reduced expectation of privacy of convicted
persons who come within the ambit of the legislation.

[
59
]
In
Have
,
supra
, Justice Duncan was concerned about the potential for prosecution
during the period of compliance, in this case for 10 years, for failing to

required. In
Clarke, supra,
the court remarked that the information
requirements are a considerable intrusion into the offender’s liberty and

In
R. v. Dyck
, supra
, the court considered the social stigma
attaching to the order to register.

[
60
]      It takes little
imagination to appreciate the concern of sex offenders for being identified by

in

, supra

save for the judgment of the police service involved.

[
61
]      Having regard to
the purposes of the Act, this discussion necessarily focuses upon the purposes
enumerated in s. 2 which addresses the
privacy interests of sex offenders and the public interest in
rehabilitation and reintegration. To that end, it is intended that information
be collected only to enable police to investigate offences of a sexual nature
and that access, use, and disclosure of the information be restricted.  There
remains within the ambit of the Act, in my view, potential for considerable
intrusion, which may be determined by the approach of persons authorized to
collect the information from the offender as well as those investigating the
commission of an offence of a sexual nature.

[
62
]      As discussed
above in the context of the impact upon the offender, the exercise of
discretion may be evidenced in the requirement upon reporting to prove one’s
identity. The person collecting the information may routinely require that

and photograph which depicts distinguishing physical characteristics. As well
an offender may experience unwanted direct or indirect encounters with the
police at his or her residence or place of employment as they investigate an
offence and consider potential suspects. These encounters may have the effect
of interfering with the offender’s rehabilitation and reintegration, especially
if they cause disruption to home or employment.

iii) the circumstances of
the individual offender

[
63
]      The offender is
54 and has a dated record for two drinking and driving convictions. He has been
involved in stable intimate relationships with adult females for some length.
He was assessed as a low risk to re-offend sexually and there is no suggestion

Conclusion and Remarks

[
64
]      As a result of
the analysis conducted, I found

that the impact of registration upon the
defendant would be grossly disproportionate to the public interest in requiring
registration under the SOIRA. In addition, I wish to remark further upon the
ambit of the exception contained in
s. 490.012(4)
, the purpose of the
legislation and in that context the significance of circumstances pertaining to
the offence and the offender, and finally the balancing approach suggested by
Cromwell J.A.
in

R. v. Jordan
, supra.

[
65
]      The legislation
permits an exception to the general rule that the perpetrator of a crime of a
sexual nature must register under the SOIRA. The onus is on the offender to
satisfy the court that the exception should be exercised.  I agree with the
view of Justice Duncan
expressed in
R. v. Have
, supra ,
and presented
with approval by Gruchy J. in
R. v. Clarke, supra
, which is that to give
meaning to
section 490.012(4)
, there must be circumstances pertaining to the
offence and the offender which qualify for exception. The circumstances of this
offence and this offender are strongly supportive of the conclusion that having
regard to the public’s interest in registration, that the impact upon him would
be such that he should not be required to register. The cases for which
registration will not be required will be infrequent, perhaps rare, however
they may not be so rare as to render s. 490.012(4) redundant.

[
66
]      It would seem
that the principal purpose of the SOIRA is to collect information pertaining to
those offenders for which there is reason to believe, either from the nature of
the offence, the background of the offender, or other pertinent information,
there is some risk to the public in future.  I see no evidence of that in this
case. The fact that Mr. Epp has not offended in this manner previously and has
been assessed as a low risk to re-offend sexually is pertinent. Certainly the
lack of a related record, the nature of the offence, and an assessment of a low
risk to re-offend sexually, are not alone determinative of this question.
However, all of this information taken together and considered as a whole in
light of the purpose and principles contained in s. 2., and having regard to
that balance that Parliament no doubt sought to achieve when it provided for a
general rule and some exception, allows for the exercise of my discretion to
grant the offender’s application.

[
67
]      There may be
other purposes to the legislation, such as the elimination of an innocent
perpetrator. However, this purpose, unlike the DNA provisions, is relatively
minor in significance, given that the data may be consulted without any
evidence pointing to or away from the offender, provided the peace officer is
investigating a specific crime of a sexual nature. As well, when comparing the
potential use of this registry to that of the DNA databank, far from
eliminating or identifying certain suspects, consultation of this registry may
widen the parameters of the investigation to include several offenders as
suspects.

[
68
]      I have looked at
this question using the approach recommended by Cromwell J.A.
in
R. v.
Jordan
, supra
, which is to compare the majority of cases against the
circumstances of the case before the court with a view to determining if these
circumstances vary markedly from the cases that Parliament may be presumed to
have had in mind in devising this registration scheme. With this in mind, I
have found the impact upon the offender to be grossly disproportionate to the
public interest behind the legislation. I say this having found that this
offence is at the low end of the range of sexual offences and very likely less
serious than any other reported decision considered herein.
